subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE MORALE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
In view of the fact that the Canadian government's relationship with public servants has deteriorated drastically in recent years, resulting in low morale, antagonistic negotiations, mass demonstrations and strike action, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle):
That this House instruct the government to do the following as initial steps in attempting to improve the situation:
(1)	To immediately reopen direct negotiations with the clerical component of the PSAC and make a more realistic offer than the 5 per cent per annum offered to these low-salaried government employees;
(2)	to grant extensions of the priority status to those former government employees who were laid off in 1978 and 1979;
(3)	to table before this House a government plan to increase government and management efficiency prior to any further lay-offs or staff size reductions; and
(4)	when government lay-offs or staff reductions are planned, to provide an itemized report on the government services that will be affected before any action is taken.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
In view of the recent statements of PQ ministers Landry and Joron, to the effect that Quebeckers should pay the world price for their oil and natural gas, which tremendous increase could be offset by exporting electricity, can the minister give the House the assurance that Canadians, and Quebeckers in particular, because they belong to Canada, should have the advantage of paying a far lower price than the world price for their oil and gas? Moreover, could he say whether the exports of electricity would make up for the high cost of oil in a sovereign Quebec?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER QUEBECKERS REMAINING IN CONFEDERATION WOULD BENEFIT FROM PAYING LESS THAN INTERNATIONAL PRICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, here again we are dealing with a
April 29, 1980

whole series of statements coming from PQ ministers that are completely groundless. In the last few years, all Canadians, and Quebeckers in particular, have benefited greatly from the fact that our price in Canada has been lower than the world price. This government has clearly indicated that we would arrive at a made-in-Canada price for oil and gas that would be lower and will continue being lower than the international price, which will be advantageous for all Canadians, including Quebeckers, as long as they belong to the country known as Canada.
In answer to the second part of the question, I would say that clearly the exports of electricity mentioned by the ministers would be totally inadequate as compensation for the world price a sovereign Quebec would have to pay. According to the best forecasts, such exports could bring in some $600 million, while oil imports at world prices would cost over $6.8 billion. What we are witnessing here is a bunch of nonsense meant, literally, to hoodwink Quebeckers in the current referendum struggle.
Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. What emphasis, in Canada's over-all energy program and policy, is the government placing on coal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are placing a high emphasis on coal. Together with the provinces which have a lot of coal, we are carrying out many examinations in this field. The hon. member knows, however, that there are certain problems in connection with coal exploitation in terms of the environment and the cost of production in some areas. These are being examined.
Currently, for instance, discussions with British Columbia are going on concerning the development of whole new areas of that province for the exploitation of coal, some of it for export. If we could count on a sufficiently high demand in Canada, I can assure the hon. member that we would want to examine the coal option very closely as being one which would be added to those arising out of our large resources of gas and other forms of energy.

I appreciate the minister's answer. I wonder if he could outline any steps the government is presently taking to deal with the great issue with regard to coal from the west and from the maritimes, and tell us in particular whether anything is being done about the gasification of coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question of the gasification of coal is one which has been examined and which is still being reviewed on an almost constant basis. I must advise the hon. member, however, that it appears at the present time that coal gasification for domestic purposes would result in a more expensive product than the large amounts of gas we already

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. But in today's paper there is a quotation from his office to the effect-to quote one of his officials-"We goofed; there is not to be such a direct service announced."
1 realize how anxious the hon. minister was to accommodate his supporter in the back benches, the hon. member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe, but if I may paraphrase the hon. member for St. John's West and indeed the minister's officials, I am sure the minister would not want to deliberately "goof with a Newf". speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me say once again that this is a continuation of my first opportunity to speak in debate this session, and I wish to join with other hon. members of the House in expressing my congratulations to you, Madam Speaker, and to offer my best wishes to you in your new responsibilities in the chair.
To continue the debate from the other evening, Bill C-19 is a very important measure with which, I submit, this House should deal with dispatch. I am delighted to refer to an intervention during my remarks the other evening by the distinguished House leader for the opposition, who indicated so openly his willingness to co-operate in the quick adoption of this most important measure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: I am a most agreeable fellow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
I believe there is complete agreement in this House that anything we can do as a government to alleviate any aspect of unemployment in this country must be done with haste and dispatch.
The other evening as time ran out for this debate I was stressing the importance of youth in this country in relation to the employment tax credit plan. The youth of this country suffer much more than their fair share in relation to unemployment, accounting for almost half of the total unemployed in Canada. The employment tax credit program has been a useful means of helping young people gain a foothold in the work force. About 55 per cent of the participants to date have been in the 25 or under age group, split equally among men and women.
There is substantial evidence to indicate that the early labour force experience of individuals has a significant bearing on their later employment and income record. Jobs obtained through this program, incidentally, have a fair chance of becoming permanent. In Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta, more than half the employers have indicated that the jobs newly created would survive beyond the 52 weeks maximum for earned tax credits. In Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec more than 57 per cent felt most of the jobs would survive, while the figure was 41 per cent in British Columbia.
In the fiscal year 1979-80 some 39,000 agreements were signed and a total of about 51,000 Canadians were placed in jobs. Small businesses employing 20 or fewer signed 75 per cent of all agreements, and 40 per cent of those were employers with a maximum of five in their normal work force. The program was an important source of jobs for women, representing 34 per cent of all placements.
As I said at the outset of my remarks the other evening, we must collectively agree to co-operate in the adoption of such measures that will bring some relief to the unemployed of this country.
We support not only this measure, particularly in relation to the Atlantic area, but as well the Canada Works program
which we hope to see the government keep in place as an important make-work, job-creation program for the coming months. In addition to this program assisting the youth in this country, we know that the Opportunities for Youth program, which is under review at the moment, will help in a very real way, along with other measures that are approved and funds that will be spent during the summer months, to create jobs for the young university people in the work force.
Small businesses in Canada have most fully accepted the employment tax credit program which is being extended as an interim measure, pending the introduction of new employment development measures to be introduced in this House by the minister in the very near future. Acceptance of tax credits by small businesses is reflected in the fact that 77 per cent of all agreements were signed with businesses employing 20 or fewer, as I mentioned earlier. I might say that I have received a good many inquiries in my own area and have had discussions with people who have made small businesses work in this country. They are very anxious to see this measure adopted by the House and implemented.
This program is attractive to employers for the very good reason that a maximum of $4,160 in tax credits can be earned for every person hired under the program. All of the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe region of Quebec are eligible for that amount. In most other urban areas in other regions employers can earn a maximum tax credit of $3,120 for each employee hired under the program, while in the remainder of the country the maximum is $3,640.
I realize that we can be as technical as we like, quoting figures and taking as much time as we want, but rather than delay the adoption of this measure I would simply like to take the opportunity of stressing the importance of the benefits that this measure will bring, particularly to the Atlantic region where we do have designated areas under the DREE program, areas where we do have extremely high seasonal unemployment.
I am delighted to have had the opportunity of participating in this debate in a positive way. I have indicated my support for this motion and hope that, with co-operation from all sides of this House, we will see the early adoption and implementation of Bill C-19, to amend the Employment Tax Credit Act.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had in this Parliament to participate in debate and I want at the outset of my remarks to offer my congratulations to you and, through you, to Madam Speaker on the ascension to your current high offices. I know both of you will discharge your responsibilities with that degree of dignity and impartiality which will do honour to all sides of this House, and which will satisfy members on all sides that the choices made were excellent ones.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Perhaps I can be forgiven if I have a sense of deja vu as I begin my first remarks here in this Parliament,
April 29, 1980

because during the previous Parliament I had the opportunity of speaking in debate only once. That intervention came during a debate on a proposal made by our government to extend rights to Canadians to a mortgage interest and property tax credit which would have given relief from high interest rates and high property taxes to millions of Canadians.
My particular intervention came in the course of an afternoon discussion on a motion which was proposed by the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), who was then just the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. He proposed a series of amendments to the legislation which would have had the effect of destroying the bill itself and preventing it from going forward. He put himself firmly on record as being opposed to extending this sort of tax relief for individual Canadian families.
As I said, I had the opportunity in that Parliament to speak only once in debate. I made my intervention on the proposal that is made by the present minister, and three days later the government fell. My sincere hope is that three days after this intervention on the minister's proposal which he is putting forward today, he will have the same success and that Canadians will have the opportunity to again change governments. Particularly when Canadians see the way in which this government has handled the whole question of management of the Canadian economy, they have cause for very deep concern.
The minister said in his introductory remarks that this bill would help create some 50,000 new jobs for Canadians. I can accept, as my colleagues can, that at a time when we have one million Canadians unemployed-and this figure does not include Canadians who have given up looking for work or native Canadians who are often not included in employment surveys-extraordinary measures must be taken to create employment when, clearly, unemployment is reaching the level that it is today.
I would like to stress that I find it ironic that this minister has brought-before this House, in his second bill, a band-aid measure to create these jobs when that minister was in the vanguard of leading the filibuster against the property and mortgage interest tax credit plan in the last Parliament. It is ironic that this minister and his colleagues in the Liberal party and their colleagues in the NDP blocked that tax relief for Canadians which would have provided a direct stimulus to the construction industry, given new jobs to the home furnishing industry, and given relief to individual families to make the goal of owning a home of their own much more affordable.
When we were in government we urged that action be taken quickly to give that sort of relief to home owners and young Canadians who wanted the opportunity to own a home of their own and were seeing that dream being snatched away from them by high interest rates. When we make that argument we were told by the colleagues of the present Minister of Employment and Immigration and members of the NDP that if a Canadian was wealthy enough to own his own home, then he was too wealthy to receive assistance from the government.
Employment Tax Credit Act
They said that the proposal was welfare for the rich and that such people were not entitled to receive a break from high interest rates.
Therefore, I find it ironic, to say the least, that this Minister of Employment and Immigration, who must share personally the responsibility for blocking that tax relief for Canadians, would get up today and argue in favour of a new tax credit program which would, in his words, create new jobs.
Tomorrow night is the last night for Canadians to file their income tax returns. Each of us should have had our tax returns in before now, but if you are like me, Mr. Speaker, you may not have. Millions of Canadians are going to be confused merely because of the efforts of the present Minister of Employment and Immigration in blocking that tax relief, because it was necessary for our government to put a provision on the income tax return which would allow Canadians to apply for that tax relief. There is no indication when one files a return that in fact the Liberal party and their friends in the New Democratic Party were successful in blocking that relief. Literally millions of Canadian families will find themselves tremendously confused when they discover that that tax break has been snatched away from them.
1 listened to the hon. member for Hamilton-Mountain (Mr. Deans) as he spoke in the debate on Thursday night. The hon. member was eloquent as he outlined the problems which face Canadians today, those in his own constituency and those across the country, with increasing lay-offs, increasing unemployment, and increasing financial strains caused by the scorched earth economic policies of this government. I was particularly struck by his comments regarding interest rates; they were very germane. He made a statement which I think would be useful to put on the record again. He said that perhaps with our interest rate policy we should encourage the building industry to again start building homes for people of average means. He pointed out that the spin-off in the home building industry is phenomenal, that 3.6 jobs are created in related industries for every job that is created in building a house. He asked us to imagine the number of jobs that would be created in related industries if we could get on with building homes for people at prices they could afford and with mortgages they could afford. That is what he said last Thursday night, as reported at page 397 of Hansard.
I recognize that the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain was not a member of this House last December when the Conservative party put forward proposals which would give relief from high interest rates and high property taxes to average Canadian families. He should recognize, however, when he speaks in this debate-bemoaning the Liberal government's high interest rate policies, that it was his present colleagues and the Minister of Employment and Immigration who were responsible for denying Canadians relief from high mortgage rates. It is not enough to express indignation about the effect upon Canadian families of these high interest rates today. Where was he then? Where were his colleagues when this government was trying to bring in provisions which would

April 29, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
give relief to Canadian families and stimulate the home construction industry?
In my own constituency, Mr. Speaker, a large number of young Canadians would like to have the opportunity to buy a home of their own but they find that they cannot do so. What would be the effects upon the economy in my constituency of stimulating the home construction industry? EIow many new jobs would be created, I ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration? What would happen at the Hotpoint plant in Orangeville which supplies goods for housing? What would be done at the GSW plant in Fergus? What would happen in the furniture building industries in my constituency-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: And Winnipeg.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
-and in Winnipeg, for that matter, if we were to give a shot in the arm to the home construction and home furnishing industries in Canada? How much more quickly we could create permanent jobs by giving incentives to Canadians so that they may recognize that Canadian dream of owning a home of their own. Yet we find that because of the Liberal party's policy in opposition, joined by the New Democratic Party, Canadians were denied that right and many millions of young Canadians will not have the opportunity to own a home of their own.
I think it is important that we ask these questions when considering a provision which would be an economic band-aid and which in the short term would create 50,000 new jobs. What was the policy of the minister and his colleagues when they were in opposition? What happened when we asked for their support for the initiatives we put forward to stimulate industry in Canada and create new jobs? What did they do on the night of December 13, when they were voting on a provision in a budget which would create small business development bonds?
In the mini-budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) last week, it is clear that he discovered the provision contained in the budget of December 13 which would have given small businesses in my constituency and across Canada a chance to get money at lower rates of interest. In essence, it would have subsidized interest rates for small businesses.
Where were this minister and his colleagues then? Where were the members of the NDP? In that budget we proposed measures which would have given stimulus to the small business sector, which is the major employer in the country just as it is in my constituency. Several months later the Minister of Finance has discovered that it was a good provision which would give some relief to small businessmen.
As a reasonable person, Mr. Speaker, I ask you if the small businessmen in my constituency would not be better off now if, instead of forcing an unnecessary $50 million election, instead of stalling these provisions, the Liberal party had decided to support those measures allowed them to be put in place.
The minister was party to a vote which prevented those measures being taken and which prevented us from keeping
small businessmen in business. Failures in the small business sector are running at an unprecedented rate this year. In each constituency small businessmen and family farms are going out of business at a rate unheard of in our history. Foreclosures on homes are running at a record level.
I put it to the Minister of Employment and Immigration that if he is genuinely concerned about the small business sector, about individual families and about creating jobs in Canada, it would have been better to allow that budget to go through. It would have kept Canadian businesses operating, it would have stimulated the economy and would have allowed Canadians to get on with creating the goods and services so necessary for a young and expanding population.
As I said earlier, we recognize that band-aid measures may be necessary when a million Canadians are unemployed. But I say to you that the only way we as a House of Commons can look at measures like this is to examine them in the context of the whole of the government's economic policies.
When the minister spoke in favour of this bill on second reading, I asked after he sat down whether he could elaborate on the job creation policies that were coming forward and how they differ from the proposals made by the previous government, the Conservative government. At that time the minister refused. I think he has a responsiblility to this Parliament and to the Canadian people to indicate what proposals he has to supplement what he is doing to attack the root problem of chronic unemployment that faces Canadian society today and which particularly disfavours young people. Half the people in Canada who are unemployed today are young people, Mr. Speaker. The unemployment rate among young people is running at twice the rate among older Canadians. I am worried that if the first experience young people have with the labour force is to be told that there is no room for their skills, that there is no need for them, it can have a serious effect upon their work habits in the future. What does this government propose, beyond these band-aid measures, to deal with this problem of unemployment, particularly among young people and native Canadians?
I think we have to recognize one fact, Mr. Speaker, when dealing with this whole question of employment. Perhaps nothing more graphically illustrates the difference in approach to unemployment between this government and the previous government, or between the New Democratic Party and the Conservative party, than our attitude toward job creation. We in this party believe that the private sector should be the engine for growth in the economy. We believe there should be long-term, well paying secure jobs in the private sector, not just band-aid proposals. Such proposals should not require increased expenditure by the federal government. They should not be short-term proposals which result in people being laid off after a few weeks' work.
If we are to attack the root causes of unemployment in Canada, we will have to attack them within the private sector. We will have to allow the private sector to expand in order to

April 29, 1980

provide the jobs so desperately needed today. It is not enough simply to propose band-aid solutions or short-term jobs, which is what the employment tax credit would do. We need permanent jobs, Mr. Speaker, which will give Canadians the opportunity of securing long-term employment.
The Canadian people want candor from the government regarding their economic policies. On December 13, they voted against the budget proposed by this party. They rejected the solutions we proposed and went through the election campaign claiming that our proposals were unacceptable to Canadians. They said that they were certainly unacceptable to them. The Canadian people then decided to give the Liberal party an opportunity to bring forward alternative solutions. Mr. Speaker, they have that opportunity now, but where are their policies? What are their spending plans? What is their energy policy? That would have a very important effect upon unemployment in my part of Ontario. By implication, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) indicated today that he is contemplating a major increase in the retail price of gasoline. That is the only way one can interpret his statement.
How different it is to listen to members of the Liberal party today compared to their speeches during the election campaign when they complained about our proposals to ensure energy self-sufficiency for Canadians-proposals which would ensure energy being available to all Canadians in the future at affordable prices. We were worried then, when we made our proposals, about the need to ensure jobs for Canadians.
Let me mention again, Mr. Speaker, the effect upon my constituency if this government's policies are followed and we allow ourselves to develop a growing dependence upon foreign sources of oil. What happens in portions of my constituency where Canadians must commute to work if we run out of gasoline? What happens if industries throughout the industrial heartland of Canada are forced to lay Canadians off? What happens to the homes in constituencies such as mine which are dependent upon energy being available? What happens to Canadian agriculture when shortages of energy develop?
What we find today more than two months after the federal election is that the Liberal party has yet to level with the Canadian people and to indicate what its policies are. This government has yet to tell the people where it intends to take us in terms of energy and what it will do to break that increasing dependency upon foreign oil which was started during 11 years of Trudeau government? What does this government intend to do to ensure that the promises are kept to provide energy to Canadians at a price that is affordable? It will not tell us.
What this government is doing is preparing Canadians in my constituency for higher prices and for shortages in the future. 1 ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration what will be the effects upon unemployment in my constituency in the future if his government's policies on energy continue as they are today. I ask the minister what will be the effect upon small business if the Liberal government is allowed to continue as it is today.
Employment Tax Credit Act
During the election campaign Liberal candidates went from coast to coast attacking our government because of what they described as high interest rate policies. I accept that interest rates during that period were high, because we were forced- due to the legacy left by 16 years of Liberal government, big spending government-to allow interest rates to rise. The clear implication of the statements made by Liberal candidates and Liberal frontbenchers during that period was that if the Liberal party were given a chance to govern, interest rates would go down in Canada.
You probably saw, Mr. Speaker, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), when he was Liberal finance critic in the last Parliament, appear on Morton Shulman's program in Toronto and give the firm, unequivocal undertaking that he would resign if the Liberal government allowed interest rates to go higher after they formed the government. Why is he with us today? Has he changed his mind? Surely this minister owes it to the people of Canada and to my constituents-because he was in my constituency during the election campaign-talking about Liberal solutions for the economy-to indicate why his opinion on interest rates has changed.
Clearly, interest rates in Canada are having a direct effect on the ability of small business and family farmers to provide jobs in this economy. It is not enough for the Minister of Employment and Immigration to propose band-aid solutions and to ignore the real root of the problem.
The Liberal party has a responsibility to indicate to Canadians and this Parliament what are their spending plans. Both the Minister of Finance with his mini-budget last week and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) when he tabled his estimates last week-refused to indicate to the Canadian people how much money this government intends to spend this year. How can we look upon any proposal dealing with expenditures by this government if it will not level with Canadians and indicate its spending intentions?
The Minister of Finance provided projections in his minibudget. He projected that the federal deficit might go up to $14.2 billion in 1980-81, as opposed to a $10.5 billion deficit projected in the Crosbie budget last December. The Minister of Finance projected that there would be a half of 1 per cent real growth in the economy as opposed to a 1 per cent real growth projected in the Crosbie budget of last December. The minister then went out of his way to say that his figures did not constitute a firm financial plan on the part of the government, that they were simply projections.
When will we have that plan? When will this government level with Canadians and tell us what it intends to do with the Canadian economy? Clearly, in the vote on the night of December 13, it was not enough for the Liberal party to simply say that they were opposed to what we were presenting in the budget. They had a responsibility to the Canadian people to come up with their own solutions and to indicate where they wished to take this country.
When the Minister of Employment and Immigration made his introductory remarks in this debate, he said that his

April 29, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
proposal today was not designed to undercut the role of the private sector. The minister continues to believe that the private sector should be creating jobs in our economy. How can the private sector be expected to increase investment in our economy if it is left with continuing drift and uncertainty on the part of the Government of Canada.
It has been a year and a half since this country has had a budget passed by Parliament. Yes this government, of which this minister is a prominent member, continues to deny Canadians leadership and continues to refuse to indicate to them what the government's economic plan is for the future.
There are ominous signs, Mr. Speaker, because in the Speech from the Throne the government gave an indication of how it differs from the approach taken by the previous government. The Clark government, of which I had the honour to be a part, believed that the time had come in Canada for governments to pay their bills, to reduce the size of the government, to bring it under control and to begin to have government of a size which was manageable by the Parliament of Canada and by the cabinet of Canada. But what we find in the Speech from the Throne is a statement that Canadians do not want smaller government, they want more efficient government.
I say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration that you cannot have fat government at the same time as you have efficient government. If you are going to be successful in having an economy that is properly managed, if you are going to have this Parliament discharging its responsibilities to scrutinize public expenditures properly, or if you are going to have a feeling that the cabinet, the elected representatives, have some control over the activities of the government, then you cannot have fat government. You cannot have government which is characterized by waste and by uncontrolled growth, and yet this is what appears to be offered to the Canadian people by this government.
I want to remind the Minister of Employment and Immigration of the commitment made by the Liberal party. Perhaps it is a mistake to do so because the Liberal party has already indicated its intention to break so many commitments that it made as a party in opposition. However, I want to remind him of a statement made by the Prime Minister on January 12, 1980, when he was leader of the Liberal party, to the Liberal campaign college in Toronto. I have a copy of his text here and this is what he said:
Our commitment is this:
-We will hold the line on government expenditure growth to under the rate of GNP.
-We will not introduce the gas tax or the mortgage scheme. This will mean more justice for our society and more money for the treasury.
-We will review the tax system to ensure that all sectors of the economy make their fair contribution to future needs.
-The deficit will be reduced-
I find that statement hard to believe even when I see those words in black and white. The Prime Minister went on to say:
-in a phased and orderly fashion, but not at the expense of jobs, growth and the attack on inflation.
-Finally, in this election campaign we pledge that any new expenditure programs to meet the evolving needs and requirements of Canadians will be financed by re-allocating existing expenditures or by increases in revenues. We will not add to the deficit by adding new programs.
I asked the President of the Treasury Board in this House last week on more than one occasion if he would level with the Parliament of Canada and with the Canadian people and indicate whether that promise to hold spending growth to less than the growth in the GNP would be kept. The minister refused to give a straight answer. He refused to give a firm undertaking that it would be. He said that that was their goal, that they would like to hold down expenditure growth to less than the real growth in the GNP. But he refused to give any firm commitment.
I ask what happened to the commitment that any new expenditures would be financed by reallocating existing resources as opposed to increasing the deficit? What will the deficit be? What are the spending plans of this government? When will the Canadian people be given the opportunity to know what plans the government has for them? When will the government level with Canadians? What does the Liberal party believe in? What kind of leadership does it intend to provide for Canadians? Surely the time has come with a majority government in office to provide leadership for Canadians and for the government to provide an example of candor if they expect the private sector is going to be willing to make the investment that is necessary to create new jobs in our economy.
I would remind the minister as well of a statement that was made by the Liberal party during the election campaign in response to a Financial Post questionnaire about spending. This is how the Liberal party responded to that questionnaire and stated their policy on spending and growth:
Our policy is to continue ensuring that government spending grows less rapidly than gross national product. As this policy will require the same kind of restraint which kept spending increases below 10 per cent over the last four years, most changes will have to be in the form of reallocations of existing budgets to ensure continued emphasis on economic development and to protect the least fortunate in society.
What happened to that commitment? If you believe that the Liberal party was serious and was acting with honesty when it made this commitment, what it must do now, when the Minister of Finance projects a real growth rate in the Canadian economy for this year of one-half of 1 per cent, is to keep spending to less than one-half of 1 per cent of real growth. Will the government keep that commitment or break it as it has broken so many others?

When will we have a budget? When will we have more than band-aid measures? When will we have an indication that the government is serious about dealing with these problems which it complained about when in opposition? What we have today in positions of leadership in Canada is a government that is either indifferent to business or hostile to it.
We can go back to the date of the Prime Minister's year end remarks when he talked about a new society, when he talked about how the free enterprise system in Canada had failed. The free enterprise system in Canada, Mr. Speaker, was not given the opportunity under successive Liberal governments to succeed. What they found was that the federal government would strangle the private sector through increasing regulation, through paperwork burden, through higher taxes, through uncontrolled federal spending which led to massive inflation on the part of the Canadian economy. Clearly Canadian business has a right to be skeptical as it makes its investment decisions for the years ahead. Surely small businessmen in my constituency have a right to ask the minister and to ask all members of the treasury bench what their plans are and when they will begin to recognize the problems facing small businessmen, family farmers and families of average means in Canada today. When will the government begin to bring in proposals which will be helpful to these Canadians? We do not see any indication of any awareness on the part of this government of the problems being faced by so many Canadians.
1 was disturbed by two aspects of this bill in particular. The first is in the area of job creation. While this will be helpful in the short term, these jobs are not necessarily permanent ones. When the parliamentary secretary spoke he tried to respond to this point by pointing out that you can roll forward the benefit for up to five years, and if a business became profitable after five years it could claim, at any time during that five-year period, this tax credit.
What he is saying is that the government intends to provide benefits for small businesses as soon as they no longer need them, as soon as they get profitable, not in the formative stages, not when times are rough, not when the jobs of Canadians who are already working in those small businesses are already in jeopardy because they are not profitable, but when they turn the corner by themselves without the assistance by this government. Then the tax credit will be of some use.
1 want to put on the record again the comments made by the parliamentary secretary because I found them extraordinary. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration said, as quoted at page 393 of Hansard:

You can call on them for your tax credit after you turn the corner, after you become profitable-if you do in spite of this government's policies.

Madam Speaker, I did not want to miss this opportunity to make some comments on the bill under consideration or on the extension of legislation that we already know. Still I would like to say to the minister at the outset that of course in principle we cannot seriously object to his request to maintain the tax credits in order to help not only some industries but more particularly a number of unemployed who would be glad to be back in the labour force. In principle we have no major objection but indeed we will not miss this opportunity to let the minister know that this measure is just not enough to solve the problem of unemployment that we face today because unemployment means a lot of hardship or misery for over a million Canadians.
This is not the first time in about 12 years or so that I have heard unemployment problems discussed in the House of Commons. I remember very well that when I first came here there was already concern about the fact there were some
300,000	unemployed. In the last 12 years, after many representations, there were so many statements or promises that that number of 300,000 would be reduced! Today there are about four times as many unemployed. 1 am concerned as are my colleagues and many others. I presume members opposite are also concerned about the means that are now open to the government, whose attitude since the throne speech gives us even more reason to worry, and thousands of Canadians are worried because of inadequate measures.
We have before us a piece of legislation that will undeniably produce a few thousand jobs, but we must not waste this opportunity to make the minister aware of the situation-in any case, he can take new initiatives in cabinet-to prod him to make proposals that would go much further than the form of aid we have before us.
I know that this legislation results in assistance ranging from $1.50 to $2 an hour in certain areas. I also know that this legislation which has been in force for over a year has meant the creation of some 50,000 additional jobs. According to the minister the problem lies in the fact that the act provided for tax credits ending March 31 and that it was urgent to table this bill which, of course, has forced the House to postpone the throne speech debate.
The minister emphasizes that, as stated in the Speech from the Throne, he definitely intends to present in the near future-perhaps in a matter of two or three weeks-other job-creation programs to deal with the unemployment problem
in Canada. I want to stress that this is only a beginning and that the government will keep introducing job-creation programs. Finally there will be a committee to study the possibility of creating new mechanisms which would help create employment. These are observations which have often been made in the House of Commons for the past 12 years, Mr. Speaker, and I do not believe that the absence of adequate measures in the Speech from the Throne must be construed as wishful thinking.
In the Speech from the Throne we have not heard many commitments on the part of the government to reassure the
200,000,	300,000 or 400,000 unemployed. In addition, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) did not hesitate to point out that unemployment would reach at least 8 per cent, and in view of the delay in tabling his budget, we already have the impression that unemployment could reach 9 per cent at the end of this year which means 200,000 or 300,000 additional unemployed. Also, the absence of economic direction will delay some investments and discourage some investors from taking concrete steps in terms of job creation. The minister must be aware of those things.
We are now clearly witnessing the economic failure of this government over the last 12 years. Mr. Speaker, some might say we did not bring in enough measures during the seven months we were in power, but we had already clearly given a new direction in terms of the use of private enterprise. It was also clear that businessmen seemed to feel we were moving toward a kind of co-operation and mechanisms that would allow them to invest with confidence and optimism because after only a few months they were already feeling we were going to give back to private enterprise the place it deserves in a society like ours. But in the circumstances, in the absence, 1 repeat, of the measures that were necessary, it is also clear that we are going to experience once again a certain stagnation that is going to create more unemployed, given the measures which we had already considered and which this government is now refusing to take.
And to illustrate this, since 1968, I think we might have to talk about a drama because I think we have to agree that in the context of unemployment, which we call the cancer of our economy, it is clearly a drama. And it is a drama at the Canadian level, it is a drama in my province also-I think many hon. members from Quebec know perfectly well the miseries the province of Quebec is going through as a result of a rather extraordinary rate of unemployment. Some would like to blame the provincial governments and heaven knows how the provincial government-even before the arrival of Mr. Levesque, Mr. Speaker, when Mr. Johnson or Mr. Bourassa was in power-was always under fire from members of this House because of the rate of unemployment back home; it was the same in the maritimes and elsewhere, and we just found out that there are problems and concerns in Ontario as well, and rightly so. So I believe that the last 12 years indicate a
April 29, 1980

failure at this level and it seems that the measures or the attitude or the theories of the current government did not succeed in finding a solution to adjust the unemployment rate to a more acceptable level.
In the light of strong disappointment, Mr. Speaker, some people wanted to take advantage of the Speech from the Throne to address themselves only to the question of national unity. I have no objection because it is a problem that has to be solved before long, but how can we think of a solution to national unity when the unemployment rate will rise again this year, when so many regions and provinces show their disappointment with the lack of sufficient measures, the lack of efforts to consult with the provinces in the face of an economic problem?

This economic failure is certainly not my responsibility nor that of my party and the proposal by the minister is nothing more than a feeble attempt at solving forthcoming problems.
I shall speak about my own province, but 1 would certainly not want to miss the opportunity to state that the same problems exist in my constituency. Since I have represented this constituency for 12 years, 1 know how many times I have had to appeal on behalf of serious organizations such as the municipal council of the major city in my riding and how many representations I have made on behalf of certain municipalities and organizations concerning economic matters. Clearly, the government refuses to give help that is essential and now urgent. And it speaks of a measure that is efficient and will reduce unemployment. they have to depend on social measures and unemployment insurance. Such claims are simply not true.

The public expects real proposals, a new economic direction; the people and the business sector are waiting for the government and the budget, to find out in what direction the country will go from here on in. It is urgent, I think, that the government recognize that middle and long-term policies and objectives are needed in terms of the private sector which would certainly appreciate knowing the intentions of the government. Then we will be able, I think, to encourage investors to invest more money. We certainly will have to have some kind of incentives so that Canadians invest their money in our businesses, instead of the government procrastinating on those measures which we will debate until May 20, Mr. Speaker. I know it, I feel it; there is now a more pressing priority than to listen again, Mr. Speaker, to questions directed to ministers about questions asked by Quebec ministers. It does not make any sense at a time when we have so much to deal with here in Ottawa.
If some members are concerned about the loss of confidence of a number of Canadians or a number of Quebeckers in the federal system, it is because the people in charge at that time lost this confidence here in the House and now they will have to win it back here in the House by introducing constructive, positive measures. The minister of employment will have his work cut out for him during the next few months and the next few years. Of course, the measure he has moved is acceptable but the lack of propositions, for which we have been waiting for three weeks, is bound to discourage Canadians. It is certainly not likely to encourage the members who sit on this
April 29, 1980

side who, I am sure, had succeeded in giving at least a direction and a certain optimism to all Canadians.

This experience has unfortunately resulted in an increase in the number of unemployed in Canada from 300,000 in 1968 to 1,300,000 in 1979 or 1980. Mr. Speaker, in rising to debate the principle of the bill now before us, Bill C-19, one is struck by what I would call the somewhat schizophrenic behaviour of the government. On the one hand, the government doles out money to business to subsidize the private sector to create jobs in the short run, as exemplified by this bill, and on the other hand, sometimes in co-operation with other governments, they hand out millions to business, again to subsidize the private sector to destroy jobs in the longer run. Obviously this bill is an example of the former, and the example to which I want to refer in just a few moments is a rather glaring illustration of the latter.
The attitude of the government would seem to be summed up rather well in the words of a rather well known actor, Peter Ustinov, when he said, "I find myself of two minds on the subject-one more or less in disagreement with the other." That appears to be the attitude of the government.
As I said, this program seems to fall into the first category-handing out money or doling out money to some of the private sector in order to create jobs in the short run. Are they temporary jobs? How temporary are they? Do we really know, as yet, how many jobs have been created by this wage subsidy program, most of which will be at the minimum wage or very close to it, I would suspect? Perhaps we could hear something more from the government as to what level of income they expect people to live on who hold the jobs which are, in large part, created by this program. Is the purpose of this bill to open up to new applicants or new businesses the addition of more employees in the creation of more production, or is it to extend the current jobs already created in that sector?
In any case, I should like to now comment on the opposite end of the pole. A story appeared in the Toronto The Globe and Mail on April 21 entitled: "$140 million grants to mills will cost 600 to 800 lost jobs". The almost $50 million, which is the federal government's contribution to this particular program, is not, to our way of thinking, in line with the recent statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the policy of the government is to "help those who need help the most". If that is the case, I think we have come upon a rather startling definition of those who are "in need" in our society.
1 should like to mention some of the companies. The article which appeared in The Globe and Mail reads as follows;

As a result, the government now has to guide it with multi-million dollar incentives.
Mr. More's words describing their attitude in past years are rather colourful, but I should like to quote his remarks as they appeared in The Globe and Mail. I am sure The Globe and Mail would not print anything which should be censored. It reads as follows:
They take the attitude: "When things are good, we'll go like a son of a bitch and make good profits, and when they're bad we'll tough it out."
Those are the words of an official of the Conservative government of Ontario describing the attitude of the compag-nies to which this government is giving $50 million because they did not do their jobs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Does that offend you?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
As a woodworker, it really offends me. But it is difficult to understand what rationale the Department of Regional Economic "Contraction" has in mind when it gives this kind of assistance to companies with that kind of dismal record in terms of looking after their own affairs and keeping their own business house in order. It is an incentive for initiative in reverse. It is free enterprise turned upside down. I am suprised that my Tory friends are not jumping in on this. Surely the Conservative government of Ontario could be wrong too.
This is one of those nice hunky-dory, cosy relationships we seem to have within the "contracted" departments and their friends. Something needs to be said because we hear some of our friends to our right chastizing some of the unemployed for refusing to accept work, by whatever definition they may choose, as one of the speakers did earlier in this debate last week.
The Conservative party was rather schizophrenic on that too, because one of their critics stood up and said that there were actually fewer unemployed than appeared because a lot of people would not take jobs when they were offered, while another stood and suggested there were in fact hundreds of thousands of hidden unemployed in Canada who should appear in the statistics but do not in fact do so. I suppose the government is not the only group that is a little schizoid in this regard.
The policies being pursued, which are creating such a severe rate of unemployment in a number of industries, particularly in the forest industry, are really the result of a coalition policy, again of the current Liberal government, the past Liberal government and the "blue blip" that appeared in between. One of the key aspects of that policy, of course, has been the continually rising-now floating-slightly sinking-we will never know-interest rate policy that has been a feature of all three governments.
1 would just like to mention a few things about unemployment, in the forest industry in particular. In fact, things are getting so standard as regards lay-offs and headlines and news about lay-offs from one end of the country to the other that the Daily Townsman of Cranbrook, in the riding of my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke
April 29, 1980

(Mr. Parker), now prints headlines that say "CFI plans no lay-offs yet due to poor market". Surely we have reached the height of absurdity and asininity in terms of our approach to unemployment and the kind of policies which seem almost deliberately designed to create it when the fact that there are no lay-offs at a major mill creates news. Surely our world is being turned upside down.
This is not just a matter of the government's current interest rate policy. I will have something more to say a little later about the designs and the plans of both the government and the Bank of Canada and its announced policies, which seem to be pursued in order to put us into an even worse position than that now prevailing in the United States. If we think we are in trouble in our housing industry, let us consider the United States lumber industry which is facing an even worse crisis. This government by its statements-and I will go into those in a few minutes-seems determined to catch up.
On April 4, just a few weeks ago, a report in a newspaper in Spokane, Washington, indicated 38,000 lumber workers in the Pacific northwest were unemployed due to high mortgage and high interest rates prevailing in the United States. In this morning's The Globe and Mail it was reported from Boise, Idaho, that more than 60,000 mill workers and lumberjacks in the northwest and southern United States are now out of work, due again to interest rate policies and the refusal of the United States government, although it has done more than the Canadian government, to take specific action to aid home owners, giving some type of assistance to those who are having to renew their mortgages for the first time. That government is doing more than Canada, but it is still only a drop in the bucket there. This government is doing nothing here.
No one would suggest, and members of this party would be the last to do so, that whatever action the Canadian government takes in terms of our mortgage interest rates, or the interest rate structure in Canada, is going to put everybody back to work in the Canadian forest industry. None of us would suggest that. There is a significant market, particularly for plywood, in central and eastern Canada, but that market is falling apart.
In a number of recent stories, one again in today's The Globe and Mail, this is mentioned. This article is from Amherst, Nova Scotia, and it states:
Tony Rumbold said markets for the bureau's 49 member-firms started dipping sharply in February as high interest rates slowed down housing construction in Canada and the United States.
That report is from the Maritime Lumber Bureau. The situation has worsened.
I am not suggesting that the unemployment statistics tell the whole story, but what are some of the statistics in the forest industry? Let me refer to the government's figures from Statistics Canada's labour force survey for March, 1980. They indicate that in the Atlantic provinces in the forest industry there were 4,000 unemployed, or 44.4 per cent. According to StatsCan there were 11,000 or 44 per cent unemployed in the forest industry in the province of Quebec, and that is as of March. In Ontario the figure was 11.1 per cent, but both the
Employment Tax Credit Act
governments of Ontario and of Canada seem set hell bent to make it worse.
In British Columbia there were 3,000 or 10 per cent unemployed, and let me say a little more right now about that 3,000 figure or 10 per cent in March for British Columbia. The last report compiled by regional Council No. 1 of the IWA which covers western Canada-these are just IWA members but there are a number of other labour organizations in the forestry industry in this country including the Canadian paper-workers union and the lumber and sawmill workers, not to mention the tens of thousands of Canadian woodworkers who do not have the benefits of union organization-listed 3,000 unemployed in the IWA alone in March, but as of April 22 the total for that region west of the Manitoba-Ontario border was 6,082.
By May 2, just a few days from now, there will be an additional 300 laid off in The Pas, Manitoba, by the Manitoba Forestry Resource Corporation. Just a couple of days ago, I believe, there were 350 people laid off at a mill in Salmon Arm, British Columbia. By the end of April 1,640 employees of Weldwood of Canada will be laid off, mainly in the Williams Lake and Quesnel areas of the Cariboo district in British Columbia. That is a total of 8,000 to 9,000 people.
Let me read briefly from a couple of notes prepared for me a few days ago when I attended a meeting that was attended in turn by a number of people who had just been laid off or were about to be laid off in the Kootenay region, both Kootenay West and Kootenay East-Revelstoke. I asked some of them for an up-to-date report. This note is from an employee of Revel-stoke Sawmill in Radium, British Columbia, and states:
On April 4, Revelstoke Sawmill, Radium, closed down "B" mill which was employing 70 people and maintenance and also laid off one shift at the planer, employing 15 people. On April 18, 1980, there were further lay-offs. The company shut down the planer. There are now only 37 people left working and this is very unstable. We suspect that within a very short time the mill will close down completely. This will leave approximately 200 people out of work. This figure does not include the contract loggers and truckers.
More of them are going down. The note continues:
This is the main industry in our area and our people are scared. There is no sign of improvement. We feel the government had better have a good look at the situation and do something about correcting it.
That is an appeal for help from real people, and this mill is in a small community. Certainly, there is a tourist industry in Radium Hot Springs. This city sits right on the edge of one of our greatest national parks. But in terms of stable year-round employment, the forest industry is all that these people have and all that many of the communities in that area have, both in the east Kootenay and in the west Kootenay and in hundreds of other smaller communities across this country. We must begin to do something about the situation.
In the town of Haney, which is found in one of the Fraser Valley ridings, there were 350 shake and shingle employees laid off due to market conditions. They expect a possible 150 more in the near future. At least 100 loggers have not returned to work, and it is possible that other mills will cut back. There

April 29, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
were 70 cedar mil! employees laid off, and all the other loggers were late in returning. Stories like that can be repeated by the hundreds.
It is not enough to have an employment tax credit creating a few temporary jobs close to the minimum wage when what we are facing across the length and breadth of this country is thousands, approaching tens of thousands, of people who work hard for their living, who are proud but are being cast on to the garbage heap of society because this government and previous governments have refused to take any concerted action to attempt to come to grips with their problems.
Sometimes statistics are sneered at. I recently read a cartoon. It was one of those cartoons which can be read, and it is not necessary to see the pictures. The cartoon was in the Castlegar News of March 22, and I believe that it was written by Jules Feiffer. The situation pictured is a little boy asking questions of a man behind a desk. On the desk is the word "Economist". It reads:
What's a depression?
Bad for business.
Yeah, but what is it?
A depression is when upwards of 12 per cent of the middle class is unemployed.
What's a recession?
Unsettling for some individuals but a useful hedge against inflation.
It sounds like government policy.
Yeah, but what is it?
A recession is when upwards of 7 per cent of the white middle class is unemployed.
What's affluence?
Good times!
Yeah, but what is it?
Affluence is when only 3 per cent of the white middle class is unemployed, and minority unemployment has levelled off at 25 per cent.
We are past that. Perhaps I am playing the role of the little boy, but I know that we are getting the same kinds of answers from this government as the economist in the cartoon gave. We got the same kind of answers from the last government- the "blue blip" between the two Liberal administrations.
One of my Conservative friends to my right had the absolute unmitigated gall recently to wonder where the New Democratic Party was when the Tory government was brought down without being given a chance to do anything in government. The Conservatives intended to give up to $375 to some home owners in Canada and to some people who wanted to buy homes. This was at the same time as their interest rate policies-and maybe the Liberals will have something to cheer about as well for a while-climbed continuously during their nine month aborted pregnancy in office, enough to raise the payments on an average home by at least $500, possibly $1,000 and probably $1,500 in a year.
The Conservatives expected us to be thankful because their government was going to give back up to $375 to some of the people. That is like suggesting that we should have confidence in the captain of a ship who sends half his crew to paint the superstructure while he sends the other half below to scuttle
the hull. The Conservatives complained, and they wanted to know where we were. I was not here but my party was here, and we were doing our job when we brought down that government because it had to be one of the worst governments in one of the shortest periods of government in the history of Canada. It was so bad that it even made the second coming of the Liberal party look good.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: No way.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: They weren't that bad.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: That's going too far.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Apparently many Canadians thought they were better. There are a number of other statistics which one could quote. I do not wish to get into them, but there are a few lessons to be learned.
I would like to go back to the joint program of the Department of Regional Economic "Contraction". All of the companies to which they gave assistance-approximately $50 million in federal dollars and $100 million in Ontario dollars, all of which were taxpayers' dollars-were large, integrated companies, and many of them were owned by multinationals. Almost all of them were companies with integrated operations, not only in lumber, but in shake and shingle, plywood and-most important for our current purposes-in the pulp and paper industry which is doing rather well at the present time.
The pulp and paper industry is the only sector of the forest industry that is showing strength at this point in our history. Why does that assistance go to the sector which should be strong? Simply to reward them for their lack of initiative in not keeping their plants up to date in the past when they were earning good money? They were doing their job badly, but they are one of the few industries that have really made it on the differential between the Canadian dollar and the U.S. dollar. It has been cream for the pulp and paper industry, and it is still doing rather well. They are the people whom this government and the Prime Minister believe need assistance most. At least, that is to whom the government is giving assistance.
I said earlier that 1 wanted to comment for a few moments on the actions of other governments. One might classify the new program for assistance to the house building industry, $160 million, in the United States as peanuts, but at least it is a start. In the context of the United States $160 million does not go very far. Nor would $16 million in a Canadian context go very far, but at least it would be a beginning.
I do not often have very much of a favourable nature to say of the present government of British Columbia, but a few months ago it became involved in a program, whatever its difficulties, in which, by using approximately $7 million, it generated $200 million in terms of mortgage loan assistance to people for new housing starts. That is perhaps one of the few and only reasons why British Columbia housing starts in the first period of this year had a slightly better performance than the rest of the country.
April 29, 1980

I am not suggesting that the federal government make a duplicate copy of the B.C. program, nor am I suggesting that it make a carbon copy of the United States program; but I am pleading with it to do something besides giving away up to S50 million to large, integrated companies that are not in difficulty for the purpose of eliminating hundreds of jobs, in this case throughout northwestern Ontario.
The Globe and Mail of today had an article in its business section headed "Bond prices spurt higher as large U.S. banks reduce prime rate to 18.5 per cent". The article is on page B3. Again, what it says is rather shocking and is an indication, I suppose, of this government's real policy at a time when it should be doing something to create demands in housing, for our forest products, lumber and plywood, to a meaningful extent within Canada through a new approach to interest rates.
The article reads in part:
The U.S. authorities' stance contrasts sharply with that of the Bank of Canada, which has re-established a painfully tight grip on the Canadian banking system and is resisting the downward move in Canadian short-term rates.
The Canadian central banks' aim is to restore-
What they call-
-a more normal spread between Canadian and U.S. interest rates as the year progresses, according to economist Michael Manford of Merrill Lynch Royal Securities Limited of Toronto.
The article goes on to quote Mr. Manford:
In all likelihood this will be accomplished by slowing the decline in Canadian prime rates until U.S. rates fall below them, he wrote in the firm's Capital Markets Letter. Thus the Canadian prime rate is likely to average 14 to 14.5 per cent by year-end, compared with 13 per cent in the United States.
At the moment we have the advantage and can try to keep our industry going a little better than theirs. Their unemployment statistics are absolutely astronomical. Why in heaven's name is the government and the Bank of Canada bent on following a policy that will drive us further and further into national bankruptcy and put tens of thousands more of our people out of work?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: It is the national Liberal employment policy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
It certainly seems to be. It is not because they have not had advice.
A Canadian Press story which appeared in the Nelson Daily News on March 6 reported in part as follows:
The government could create 100,000 additional jobs through a reduction in interest rates and some fiscal stimulus, says the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy in a study released Wednesday.
Fiscal stimulus refers to tax cuts or incentives, or both.
It goes on to suggest that the government should be taking deliberate action to lower interest rates. This is in line with what the New Democratic Party has been trying to get across for some time. It would turn the whole thing around.
The International Woodworkers of America met with the previous government but 1 do not think they have yet had a
Employment Tax Credit Act
chance to meet with the present government. They presented a rather comprehensive brief to the former prime minister which discussed the impact of current interest rates on the wood products industry in British Columbia. It is a rather detailed brief of some 25 pages and accompanying statistics. It offered a well presented and documented argument and attempted to persuade the government of the day to reverse its disastrous policy on interest rates. I suggest it should be required reading for members of this government. They have heard the arguments and the facts.
Some of the top economists as well as influential groups and economic bodies in the country have suggested that the government turn its policies around. Instead of that, what we get is a renewal of the employment tax credit program. Thousands of people are being thrown out of well-paid jobs-people with mortgages, people with families, with bills to pay, with credit cards-yet incentives are still being given to finance companies, credit card companies and others so that they can advertise and increase the demand for credit. We have been suck-ered by an industry which our public policy tends to assist in this endeavour. The present policies will throw thousands of people out of work and a continuation of the tax credit program will only offer some of them temporary jobs at or near the minimum wage. That is not good enough, Mr. Speaker.
People who have been used to earning $10, $11 or $12 an hour are not fussy about accepting a short term job and losing their right to unemployment insurance benefits in order to take it. If they do not, then, of course, our Conservative friends and perhaps a couple of hon. members opposite are going to accuse them of being welfare bums who do not want to work!
Who should have to work at those rates, Mr. Speaker, in a country that has the potential and, hopefully, the ability to get its act together and produce wealth per capita such as no other country in the world can dream of? To ask our people to live below the poverty level is worse than ridiculous; it is almost criminal.
My colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) borrowed a phrase from me the other day. Indeed, I invited him to use it and he did to open his address. I should like to close with the same quotation. As the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain thought it suitable to open the subject, I, too, can think of no better phrase with which to close. Perhaps even some of my Conservative friends would listen to John Foster Dulles, who said that "the measure of success is not whether you have a tough problem to deal with, but whether it is the same problem you had last year".
We not only have the same problem we had last year, Mr. Speaker, we have a worse one. We seem bound and determined, as a matter of deliberate public policy, to further complicate it and make it worse. We go off in both directions, Mr. Speaker. We appear to have a schizophrenic government.
Perhaps I should wonder if the words of Frank Scott in his poem about Mackenzie King are not somewhat appropriate. He wrote that "We had no shape because he would not allow

April 29, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
us to take sides, and no sides because he would not allow us to take shape".
Do we have a jellyfish? Maybe, Mr. Speaker, but we do not need a jellyfish. We need a government that takes some hard, tough decisions and begins to move this country in a direction where people who want to work can work, where people who want homes can have homes, good jobs with good rates of pay. It can be done if the government will listen to some of the advice offered, not only by the opposition but by many of their own so-called experts.
1 plead with the government to listen; I plead with the government to act. I plead with them to get their act on track and try to be just a little more consistent in the pursuit of their economic policy.
